posts.title: Before a tablet goes into the yoghurt
posts.insight: Hiding medicines in food was common and usually unrecorded in a Norwegian nursing home study. Before any medicine is hidden, ask whether it is still needed and whether a pharmacist has checked it can be crushed or mixed.
posts.angle: Covert administration is sometimes right, but the first steps are to stop what no longer helps and to check each remaining medicine with a pharmacist; the documented capacity and best-interests process is stated as professional judgement.
posts.position_basis: mixed: prevalence and documentation figures are empirical (Kirkevold 2005); the pharmacist checks are from a consensus tool; the requirement for a written capacity and best-interests decision is ethical and professional judgement

captions.x:
In a Norwegian study, about 1 in 9 residents in ordinary nursing home units, and 1 in 6 in dementia units, had medicines hidden in food or drink during one week.

The practice was written in the record in only 4 in 10 cases. The data are old and Norwegian; UK figures may differ.

Before a tablet goes into the yoghurt, ask two things. Is this medicine still needed? Has a pharmacist checked that it can be crushed or mixed? Coated and modified-release tablets, and bitter ones, may be unsuitable.

We should hide a medicine only after a written capacity assessment and best-interests decision, with the family and prescriber involved and a review date set.
captions.linkedin:
In a Norwegian study of 1,926 nursing home residents, about 1 in 9 in ordinary units, and 1 in 6 in dementia units, had medicines mixed into food or drink at least once in one week.

The practice was written in the record in only 4 in 10 cases (96 of 241).

These are old Norwegian data, and UK figures may differ. No UK prevalence figure was found. The pattern is still worth checking in any care home: how often are medicines hidden, and is each case written down?

Before a tablet goes into the yoghurt, two questions come first.

1. Is this medicine still needed? Every medicine stopped is one less to hide.

2. Has a pharmacist checked this medicine? Pharmacists look at whether a tablet is coated or modified-release, and how it tastes, before it is crushed or mixed into food. Crushing can change how some tablets work, and a bitter taste can spoil the whole meal.

Hiding a medicine from a person who lacks capacity to decide about it is sometimes the right thing to do. In my judgement it should happen only after a written capacity assessment and a best-interests decision, with the family, the prescriber and a pharmacist involved, a plan for each medicine, and a date to review it.

Would the medicines being hidden in your service today pass that test?

In a Norwegian nursing home study, about 1 in 9 residents in ordinary units had medicines hidden in food or drink in one week. Only 4 in 10 cases were recorded.

Before hiding a tablet: is it still needed, and has a pharmacist checked it can be crushed or mixed?

posts.title: The tablet stopped in hospital that came back
posts.insight: Unintended medicine discrepancies after discharge affect about half of adults across studies. A stopped medicine can return by a route such as the GP repeat list or an order already placed, so someone has to own the reconciliation.
posts.angle: Use the review median for scale, show one route as a labelled illustrative example, and recommend a named person for reconciliation.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the discrepancy rate is empirical (Alqenae 2020); the repeat-list route is an illustrative example, not a measured frequency; the named-person recommendation is judgement

captions.x:
Across 11 studies in a systematic review, a median of about half of adults had at least one unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital. Rates varied widely between studies.

An illustrative example of one route: the hospital stops a tablet. The care home chart changes that day. The GP repeat list still carries it, and next month's order went in before the letter arrived. The tablet comes back in the new supply.

For every discharge with a changed medicine list, we should name one person to update the repeat list and check the next pharmacy order within days.
captions.linkedin:
Across 11 studies in a systematic review, a median of about half of adults had at least one unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital. The rates varied widely, from about 4 in 10 to 3 in 4 in the middle half of studies, and definitions differed.

The review did not look at care homes alone, and it did not measure the routes by which discrepancies happen. One route is easy to picture.

An illustrative example, not a measured case:

1. The hospital stops a tablet and says so in the discharge letter.
2. The care home changes its medicines chart that day.
3. The GP repeat list is held on a different system and still carries the tablet.
4. Next month's order was placed before the letter was read.
5. The tablet arrives in the new supply and goes back on the chart.

Each handover, hospital to home, home to GP, GP to pharmacy, is a separate chance for the change to be lost.

In my judgement, every discharge with a changed medicine list needs one named person who updates the GP repeat list and checks the next pharmacy order within days. That person should be written in the discharge plan.

Who owns that task in your area?
captions.bluesky:
Across 11 studies, a median of about half of adults had an unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital.

A stopped tablet can return if the GP repeat list or next order is not updated. Every changed list needs one named person to reconcile it.
captions.threads:
Across 11 studies in a systematic review, a median of about half of adults had at least one unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital, with wide variation.

One illustrative route: the hospital stops a tablet, the care home chart changes, but the GP repeat list and next month's order still carry it.

Every discharge with a changed medicine list needs one named person to reconcile it within days.

posts.title: What 'potentially avoidable' admission counts
posts.insight: Potentially avoidable admission rates are counted from lists of diagnosis codes, and different lists give different totals. They help compare and plan services; they do not decide whether one resident should go to hospital.
posts.angle: Explain the construction of the measure and argue against its use as pressure on individual transfer decisions.
posts.position_basis: mixed: code-based construction (Purdy 2009), use as a service measure (Lloyd 2019) and the review's framing (Chambers 2023) are sourced; the position against using the rate to discourage individual transfers is ethical judgement

captions.x:
'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes. Different lists give different totals: in one English analysis, the NHS list used 19 of the 36 conditions found in the literature.

The rates are used to compare services and programmes for care homes. That is a fair use.

A 2023 systematic review noted that admissions from care homes are often necessary, and that do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.

A code-based rate should guide planning. It should never be used to discourage transfer of a resident who needs and wants hospital care.
captions.linkedin:
'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes. The label is attached to a condition, such as a type of infection or a long-term illness, rather than to a judgement about one person.

Different lists give different totals. In one English analysis of emergency admissions, the NHS list used 19 of the 36 conditions found in the literature, and the choice of list changed how many admissions were called avoidable.

The rates are used to compare services and programmes for care homes. An evaluation of enhanced support for care homes in England used them as an outcome. That is a sensible use: a high rate points to where GP support, medicine review and prevention could improve.

A 2023 systematic review of ways to reduce unplanned admissions from care homes noted that such admissions are often necessary, and that do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic. Advance care planning was part of most programmes that worked.

The measure becomes harmful if it turns into pressure on the night nurse or the out-of-hours doctor deciding about one person.

In my judgement, a code-based rate should guide planning and should never be used to discourage transfer of a resident who needs hospital treatment and wants it. The decision for one person rests on their condition and their wishes, recorded in advance where possible.
captions.bluesky:
'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes, and different lists give different totals.

The rate helps plan care home support. It should never be used to stop a resident who needs and wants hospital care from going.
captions.threads:
'Potentially avoidable' admissions are counted from lists of diagnosis codes. Different lists give different totals.

The rates help compare services for care homes. A 2023 review noted that admissions from care homes are often necessary, and do-not-hospitalise orders were problematic.

posts.title: A year in a care home: reading the figure
posts.insight: In one study of care home residents in England and Wales, about 74 in 100 were alive a year later. A group figure like this describes many people and can't tell a family how long their relative will live.
posts.angle: Give the figure with its setting and limits, explain why death rates are higher in nursing homes, and send families to the clinician for a personal estimate.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the one-year figures and nursing versus residential difference are empirical (Shah 2013); the median definition is standard; the advice not to treat group figures as a personal prognosis is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
About 74 in 100 older people living in care homes in England and Wales in 2009 were still alive a year later. About 26 in 100 died within the year.

Death rates were higher in nursing homes than in residential homes. This most likely reflects how ill people already are when they move in; the study did not test the reason.

These figures count people already living in homes, not from the day they moved in, and they describe a group.

If your relative is moving into a care home, ask their doctor what they expect for this person. A group figure can't answer that.
captions.linkedin:
About 74 in 100 older people living in care homes in England and Wales in 2009 were still alive a year later. About 26 in 100 died within the year.

For comparison, about 3 in 100 older people living in their own homes in the same study died within the year. The two groups were not matched for age, so this is not a like-for-like comparison.

Death rates were higher in nursing homes, which provide nursing care on site, than in residential homes. After allowing for age and sex, both were well above the general population. The higher figures most likely reflect how ill people already are when they move in; the study did not test the reason.

Two limits help you read these numbers.

First, the study counted people who were already living in a home in 2009, some for years. It did not follow people from the day they moved in.

Second, any group figure describes many people. A median survival, for example, only means half the group lived longer than that and half lived less. It does not tell you about one person.

If your relative is moving into a care home, and you want to know what to expect, ask their doctor what they expect for this person, and ask again if their health changes.

More posts in the Reading the evidence series take one statistic at a time and show what it can and can't tell you.

About 74 in 100 older care home residents in England and Wales in 2009 were alive a year later. Death rates were higher in nursing homes, most likely reflecting how ill people are on arrival; the study did not test why.

A group figure can't predict one person. Ask the doctor what they expect.

posts.title: Reablement: widely offered, little tested
posts.insight: Reablement is short-term help at home to do everyday things for yourself again. Trials so far leave us uncertain whether it helps more than usual home care, which is a gap in the evidence rather than proof that it fails.
posts.angle: Lay out the three pieces of evidence, both directions, and give the person offered reablement specific questions to ask.
posts.position_basis: mixed: definition and evidence are empirical (Cochrane 2016, Tuntland 2015, Hogstedt 2026); the call for written goals and better trials is judgement

captions.x:
Reablement is short-term help at home, usually lasting weeks rather than months, to help you do everyday things for yourself again, working towards goals set with you.

The evidence is thin. A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials and was very uncertain whether it helps more than usual home care. One small Norwegian trial of 61 people found they rated their chosen activities somewhat better, but not physical capacity or quality of life. A 2026 pooled review showed no clear difference, at low certainty.

That means we don't know.

If you are offered it, ask for your goals in writing, how long it lasts, whether there is a charge, and a review at the end.
captions.linkedin:
Reablement is short-term help at home, usually lasting weeks rather than months. It aims to help people do everyday things for themselves again, such as washing, dressing or making a meal, working towards goals set with them.

It is widely offered. The trial evidence is thin, and it points in more than one direction.

1. A 2016 Cochrane review found only 2 trials, with 811 people, and was very uncertain whether reablement helps more than usual home care.

2. In one small Norwegian trial of 61 people, those offered 10 weeks of reablement rated their own performance of activities they had chosen as somewhat better at 3 and 9 months. It did not show a clear difference in physical capacity or quality of life.

3. A 2026 review that pooled reablement trials did not show a clear difference in chosen daily activities or physical performance. The certainty of the evidence was low to very low, and the pooled numbers were small.

That is a gap in the evidence. It means we don't know, which is different from knowing it does not work.

For practitioners, the Norwegian trial measured goals people chose themselves, which is a reason to set those goals and review against them.

If you or a relative are offered reablement, ask:
What goals will it work on? Can I have them in writing?
How long will the help last?
Is there any charge?
Who reviews progress at the end, and what happens next?

We also need larger trials of reablement in the UK.
captions.bluesky:
Reablement is short-term help at home to do everyday things for yourself again. Trials leave us unsure whether it beats usual home care: a gap, not proof it fails.

If offered it, ask for written goals, how long it lasts, any charge, and a review at the end.
captions.threads:

posts.title: Write the plan for the clinician who comes at night
posts.insight: An anticipatory care plan helps only if the out-of-hours or emergency clinician can see it and it contains the decisions they need. In one Scottish study, many Key Information Summaries lacked resuscitation status or preferred place of care.
posts.angle: Write for the out-of-hours reader and check that the shared record carries the decisions; Scottish data show the gaps.
posts.position_basis: mixed: KIS role and content gaps are empirical (Finucane 2019); writing for the out-of-hours reader is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Write the anticipatory care plan for the clinician who meets the person for the first time, at night.

In Scotland, the Key Information Summary is a shared record that out-of-hours and emergency clinicians can see. A plan written there can reach whoever turns up.

In one study of people with advanced illness who died in 2017, about 1 in 3 summaries did not record resuscitation status and nearly half did not record preferred place of care.

Before you close the record, read it as a stranger would. Could they act on it?
captions.linkedin:
Write the anticipatory care plan for the clinician who meets the person for the first time, at night.

An anticipatory care plan sets out what to do if someone becomes unwell, which treatments they would and would not want, where they would prefer to be cared for, and who to call.

In Scotland, the Key Information Summary (KIS) is a shared electronic record available across healthcare settings. It gives clinicians essential information for people likely to need emergency or out-of-hours care. A plan written there can reach whoever turns up.

A study of 18 Scottish general practices (Finucane et al., Br J Gen Pract 2019) looked at people with advanced progressive illness who died in 2017. About 7 in 10 had a KIS. Of those summaries, about 1 in 3 did not record resuscitation status, and nearly half did not record preferred place of care.

These were people near the end of life, not all care home residents or housebound people, and the data are from 2017. The gaps are still a useful check for any practice.

Before you close the record, read it as a stranger would:
Does it say what to do if the person becomes unwell tonight?
Does it record resuscitation status and the treatments they would not want?
Does it name their preferred place of care and who to phone?

posts.title: A care worker's report needs a reply
posts.insight: Early-warning tools for care homes only help if what care workers report is acted on and fed back. A large US trial of implementation support showed no clear drop in admissions, so services should judge these tools by the response loop.
posts.angle: Centre the feedback loop: a named person responds and tells the care worker what happened; note RESTORE2 and the training concerns for night and temporary staff.
posts.position_basis: mixed: INTERACT trial result and RESTORE2 staff views are empirical; the value of the care worker's observation and the feedback loop are judgement

captions.x:
We should treat a care worker's report that a resident is eating less, sleeping more or seems unlike herself as clinical information.

Tools exist to structure it. RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is used in UK care homes; staff in one study worried about training night and temporary staff.

In a US trial across 85 nursing homes, training staff in the INTERACT tools did not show a clear drop in admissions overall.

In my judgement, the test of any tool is simple: a named person responds, and tells the care worker what happened.
captions.linkedin:
We should treat a care worker's report that a resident is eating less, sleeping more or seems unlike herself as clinical information.

Care workers see residents every day. The person holding that observation is often the least senior person in the building, with the weakest route to a nurse or GP.

Tools exist to give that observation a structure. RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is used in UK care homes. In an interview study, care home staff strongly supported it but worried about the training needed, especially for night and temporary staff.

The evidence on outcomes is mixed. In a US randomised trial across 85 nursing homes and about 37,000 residents, training and support to use the INTERACT tools did not show a clear drop in hospital admissions overall. The trial tested support for putting the tools in place, and uptake varied.

So a tool on its own is not enough. In my judgement, services should judge these tools by what happens after the report:

1. A named person must respond, on every shift.
2. That person tells the care worker what was done.
3. Night and agency staff get the same training and the same route.

Does the care worker who raised a concern in your service hear what happened next?
captions.bluesky:
A care worker's report that a resident is eating less or seems unlike herself is clinical information.

In a US trial of 85 nursing homes, training in early-warning tools did not clearly cut admissions. The test is whether someone responds and reports back.

posts.title: Housebound and missing from the list
posts.insight: People who can no longer get to the surgery can drop out of routine reviews. Telling the practice you are housebound, and asking what can be done at home, helps keep you on the list.
posts.angle: UK researchers describe housebound patients as under-served and under-studied; a small Glasgow study found most had missed reviews. Give three specific requests to make.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the researchers' description and the Glasgow finding are empirical (framing statements and a small study); the advice to ask and the view that practices should plan home care are judgement

captions.x:
Once you can no longer get to the GP surgery, routine reviews can stop without anyone deciding they should.

UK researchers describe housebound patients as a group who find it hard to get GP care, have complex needs, and have been little studied.

In one small Glasgow study, 23 of 25 housebound people had missed routine reviews of their long-term conditions since becoming housebound.

Tell the practice you are housebound, and ask which reviews, medicine checks and vaccines can be done at home.
captions.linkedin:
Once you can no longer get to the GP surgery, routine reviews can stop without anyone deciding they should.

General practice is organised around people coming in. UK researchers describe housebound patients as a group who find it hard to get GP care, have complex needs, and have been little studied. One team called older housebound people a neglected group in research and in clinical care.

The best figure available is small. In a study of 25 housebound people in two Glasgow practices, all taking five or more medicines, 23 had missed routine reviews of their long-term conditions since becoming housebound. Between them they had missed 91 reviews. This was a selected group in deprived areas, so it does not tell us how common this is across the UK.

If you, or someone you look after, can no longer get to the surgery, three requests are reasonable:

1. Ask the practice to record that you are housebound.
2. Ask which reviews, medicine checks and vaccines can be done at home, and who will do them.
3. Ask who will contact you when a review is due.

In my judgement, practices should keep an up-to-date list of housebound patients and plan their routine care at home. People who can't come in are owed the same care as people who can.
